title: Relinquishing the Initiative
subtitle: Win material, weather the storm, then strike back

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter IV, §23 Relinquishing the Initiative, Example 53

steps.title: An exchange offer takes shape
steps.source: From the Havana International Masters Tournament, 1913. Ruy Lopez. White J. R. Capablanca. Black D. Janowski.

narration.say: Capablanca plays White against Janowski. The opening is a Ruy Lopez.
White castles. Black supports the centre with d6, and White exchanges the bishop for the knight.
White challenges the centre and develops the other knight.
After the central exchange, White develops the queen and brings the rook to d1.
Bishop to g5. Black moves the queen to e8. White plays knight to h4, and Black advances g6.
The advance of the g-pawn allows the bishop to reach h6. Black offers material in return for time and attacking chances.

steps.title: Accept the challenge
steps.source: Black offers the exchange in order to gain time and to obtain an attack.

narration.say: White brings the bishop to h6, attacking the rook on f8.
Black moves the knight to c5. White protects the second rank with the rook, and Black brings a rook to b8.
White retreats the knight to d1. Black's rook comes to b4, provoking the advance of the c-pawn.
White plays c4. Black brings the knight to e6, preparing to occupy d4.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Take the rook that Black has offered.

feedback.*: The bishop on h6 attacks the rook on f8. Capture it, then prepare to defend.

exercise.success: 17. Bxf8. White wins the exchange, but Black will have the initiative.

steps.title: Material is not the same as safety

narration.say: The knight comes to e3. Black occupies the central outpost on d4.
White withdraws the queen to d1. Black plays c5, supporting the knight.
White plays b3. Black returns the rook to b8, making room for the bishop.
Knight to f3. Black advances f5, and the exchange of pawns opens attacking lines.
Black's attack is approaching its full force. White must defend coherently, not try to spend the extra material immediately.

steps.title: Prepare the counter-action
steps.source: In reality Black's attack is reaching its maximum force. Very soon it will reach the apex, and then White, who is well prepared, will begin his counter action.

narration.say: White retreats the knight to f1. Black advances f4.
White exchanges the central knight. Black recaptures with the c-pawn.
Queen to h5. Black develops the bishop to b7.
The rook comes from a1 to e1. Black advances c5, strengthening the centre.
White plays f3. This stabilises the position and helps prepare a central exchange.
Black brings the rook to e8. White doubles rooks on the e-file, and Black lifts the rook to e6.

steps.title: Give material back to end the attack
steps.source: Now the Black Rook enters into the game, but White is prepared. It is now time to give back the exchange.

narration.say: White does not have to keep the extra exchange forever. Returning it now can remove an attacker and win a central pawn.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Return the exchange by taking the pawn on e5.

feedback.*: The rook on e2 can take e5. After the bishop recaptures, the other rook will take the bishop.

exercise.success: 29. Rxe5! White gives back material to break up the attack.

steps.title: Trade the danger for a favourable ending

narration.say: The other rook takes the bishop on e5. Black brings the rook to h6.
White offers the queen exchange with check. Black accepts, and the rook recaptures.
Black moves the king to f7. White returns the rook to e5, and Black shifts the rook to c6.
The queens are gone. White has emerged a pawn ahead, but the ending still requires accurate play.
White plays knight to d2. Capablanca notes that rook to f5 might have been better.
Both sides improve their pieces. The rook attacks d4 and the knight centralises.
White takes the pawn on c5. Black finds a strong resource: d3.
White brings the king to f2. Black exchanges the bishop for the knight, then captures the pawn on e4.
White returns the rook to d5. Black brings the rook to e3.
This rook ending is not an automatic win. White must deal with Black's advanced pawn and find an active plan.

steps.title: An active move before the adjournment
steps.source: The ending is very difficult to win. At this point White had to make the last move before the game was adjourned.

narration.say: Capablanca chooses a queenside pawn advance. It creates a new point of contact while the rook remains active.

exercise.prompt: Follow Capablanca's ending plan: advance the b-pawn to b4.

feedback.*: The b-pawn can advance two squares. White creates queenside play instead of waiting passively.

exercise.success: 41. b4! White keeps the ending active.

steps.title: Remove the passed pawn and attack

narration.say: White captures the advanced pawn on d3. Black takes the pawn on c4.
The rook swings to h3. Black takes b4, and White captures h7.
Black brings the king to f6. White takes a7, and Black advances the king to f5.
White activates the king on f3. Black's rook comes to b2.
Rook to a5, check. Black's king retreats to f6.
White brings the rook to a4. Black moves the king to g5, and White captures the pawn on f4 with check.
Black takes a2. White advances h4 with check, driving the king to h5.
Rook to f5, check. The king retreats to h6, and White advances g4. Black resigns.

steps.title: Material, defence, counter-action
steps.source: Once the material advantage is obtained, submit to the opponent's attack for a while, and once it has been repulsed act quickly with all your forces and win on material.

narration.say: Winning material may mean giving your opponent the initiative. That is acceptable only if you can withstand the attack.
White defended with a plan, then returned the exchange to remove attackers and simplify.
The ending still demanded care. Active rook play and the arrival of the king finally converted the advantage.
Do not cling to extra material when returning some of it can give you a safer and more favourable position.
